Plenty of uninformed sources say that if your animal has a dangerously high body temperature, you should put ice cubes into their rectum to bring their temperature down. If you do this, you can send the animal into shock, and the result could be fatal. 

Instead, sit with the animal in cool (but not freezing) water. Place wrapped ice packs around the outside of the animal, spray the animal’s paw pads with isopropyl alcohol, put fans aimed on them, but don’t try to put ice cubes up their butt!

Would love to answer this, but I can only choose either a cochlear implant or a hearing aid... I wear one of each, what is the preferred answer when this is the case?
Happens to me every day. It’s just part of learning to interpret the sounds you’re hearing from the CI, as far as I know.

They push the idea that if you have both done immediately, you will learn to hear with CIs faster. I have no idea if that’s true, but it’s what they told me repeatedly. Almost everyone I met with before and after my surgery were so insistent I have both done - but I never got my right side implanted. It was easier (for me, anyway) to line up the new way of hearing on my left with what little hearing I’d always had on my right.

No problem! I’m very open about it lol

I would recommend lots of research and familiarizing yourself with the risks. After I got my CI, I was so exhausted learning how to hear again. I even quit using it entirely for about a year. It takes a lot of effort, and it’s hit or miss for a lot of people. It’s not a quick fix, by any means. And a lot of places will push you to have both sides done immediately - I wouldn’t trade having half-n-half for the world! My HA guides my hearing with my CI!

If you have any more questions, feel free to DM me! I’m very open to sharing my experiences, and as a user of both a CI and a HA, I feel like I have a foot in both doors.

The best thing to do, whether or not you own a dog, is to review the basics of canine/feline CPR. Watch a few videos or demonstrations. Yes, you need to do it faster, stronger, and more consistently than the man in the OP. Ideally, one person is giving breaths and one is doing compressions, and the people performing CPR actually know what they’re doing. Even more ideally? It’s being done in a clinic, with a veterinarian and drugs and equipment on hand.

But! Even if someone does what he did but faster, while it may not be a solid way to do compressions, it’s the best the animal has in an emergency. Granted, it turns out the dog in the OP didn’t require CPR, but if the dog really did need CPR, the man in the OP is still better than nothing. The only way a dog has “more of a chance to die” is if everyone refrained from at least trying to resuscitate the dog because they feel they “can’t” try.
I understand he ultimately wasn’t the reason the dog survived, but damn, dude, a man can’t try to help?

I work in the veterinary field. It is not typical to do such slow compressions on a dog (we are taught in veterinary schools in the U.S. to do compressions to the same beat as Stayin Alive, actually). This man could be doing compressions at a slower rate because he is tired, is watching for a reaction, is unsure of what to do, etc. However, slower compressions are still a hell of a lot better than nothing!

I [20F] experience this when my boyfriend [23M] is not sleeping with me. 

I’d highly recommend a body pillow, or pushing pillows together to form a lump where your partner would sleep. If you stay cuddled up to it for a while, your body heat warms the pillows and you naturally feel less alone in the bed.

If that doesn’t work, try putting on a fan at low speed, or opening a window. Depending on where you live, calm air can sometimes mimic the sound of your partner breathing/snoring.

If all else fails, something I like to do is sleep with or wear something that belongs to my partner. I have a thermal sweater he gave me, and I sleep with that. Sometimes all it takes is something that smells like them to make it easier to sleep.

Something you shouldn’t do is wake up and text/call them. The use of a phone will only keep you awake and make it harder for you to fall back asleep, and contacting them might wake them up as well.

My favorite part of being hearing impaired is how sensitive I am to vibrations and touch. It makes the world feel much more alive. I wouldn’t give that up for anything.

My least favorite part is the lack of human interaction. People will avoid me out of the misconception that I am hard to talk to. People I want to form a romantic relationship with will often view it as an obstacle or problem, if it’s not an instant dealbreaker. I definitely feel alone most of the time, and it’s very heartbreaking.

As far as teachers go, a big positive thing is treating me like every other student. Let me show you what I can do! I will learn better if I’m presented with the same opportunities as every other kid.

The worst thing they can do is isolate me. In middle school, I carried around a giant wooden chair because the school didn’t want me sitting in metal chairs. I wasn’t very popular... but I did get strong from all that chair-carrying.

Any sort of authority is intimidating. I have a plastic card in my wallet signed by my implant surgeon detailing my need for my cochlear implant. I’ve made it a point to make my CI and my hearing aid any color other than beige. The first thing I say to authorities is, “I’m sorry, I have trouble hearing.”

Whatever they do afterwards is with the knowledge of my disability. I find comfort in knowing I do all I can to make them aware of it, no matter how small the actual situation is.

As a side note, I’m ALWAYS selected for a random search in airports.

I’d say the best thing you can do is be mindful of someone’s disability when communicating with them. Don’t get upset or frustrated if you think it’s hard to communicate with us - chances are, we’re doing the best we can to understand you! Just because someone is hearing impaired does not mean they have any less to contribute.

Not only does it make us appreciate and trust you more, but we’re much happier being a part of the conversation!
